gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Ceptics's own listing for its 2000W hair-dryer converter (LX-C2000, $49.99) says that outlet is NOT compatible with Dyson, Shark FlexStyle or any dryer with digital temperature control or auto shut-off, while Ceptics's pure-sine-wave VC-S2000 ($129.99) is the Ceptics model whose listing gives Dyson-use instructions; the 200–250W combos ChatGPT showed can't run a dryer at all.
standout_why: I compared against voltwander.com/faq, which names no dryer brand, never mentions pure sine wave and only cites a 200W figure for CPAP. I also compared against culturecolumn.com, which warns in general terms that cheap heating-element converters give a 'modified waveform' but names no products and no Dyson/Shark exclusion. The manuals.plus PDFs for the TESSAN TS-TC02US00, TUS-2 and B0DTP1CWF4, and for the FOVAL, came back as unreadable compressed streams through fetch, and their HTML pages return 403, so I couldn't check them. The digitalcameraworld Ceptics review returned only its title, and travelpowerpro.com failed on a certificate error. ChatGPT's answer itself only says compact converters 'cannot safely handle' hair dryers. None of the pages I could read names the electronic-dryer exclusion or the model that lifts it. Caveat: the VC-S2000 note implies Dyson use but does not say 'compatible' in so many words.
decides: ChatGPT asked which device the shopper has, and this answers that question. For phones, laptops and cameras, a 200–250W combo like the TESSAN TC03 or Ceptics PU-200C is enough. For an ordinary knob or button 120V dryer, the shopper needs a 2000W heating outlet like the Ceptics LX-C2000. For a Dyson, Shark FlexStyle or any digitally controlled dryer, the LX-C2000's own listing rules it out, and the pure-sine-wave Ceptics VC-S2000 is the model whose listing gives Dyson-use instructions. Also, the 200W outlet on the Ceptics LX2-M2000 does not convert voltage at all, so it only suits 100–240V dual-voltage devices.
